title: Biwa (Japanese four-string lute)
summary: The biwa is a Japanese lute with a broad pear-shaped body, a short neck and four silk strings. It is struck with a large wooden plectrum rather than plucked, and its few tall frets let a player press between them to bend a note upward. For centuries it has accompanied storytellers and court music alike.
howToPlay: Four strings run down the short neck, the lowest on the left. Each lane marks where a note is played, from the open string to the fourth tall fret.
A bead slides down the string to its place. Strike the lane as the bead lands.
The notes come from a five-note scale with half steps, so neighbouring lanes can sit very close in pitch.
Try the slow telling line first, then the bold strike-and-answer, then the bending phrase.
rules: The scale is D, E flat, G, A and B flat, in two octaves.
Every phrase is played through twice.
A strike on the beat is perfect, a near one is good, and extra strikes cost points.
The slow phrase leaves long pauses: wait for the bead.
heritageNote: Biwa players have told stories and played for audiences in Japan for over a thousand years. Makers still carve the pear body from a single block and set the tall frets by hand, so each instrument has its own voice.
credits: Tradition: the Japanese biwa; phrases written for this game
